questions.question: Rice is grown as a commercial crop in Haryana and Punjab, but as a subsistence crop in Odisha. Using your understanding of geographical factors and economic practices, explain why rice cultivation differs in these regions.
answer_steps: Climate and irrigation: Haryana and Punjab have well-developed canal and tubewell irrigation, so high-yielding rice can be grown on a large scale; Odisha's rice is mostly rain-fed under a monsoonal climate, with fewer large irrigation systems.

Economic factors: in Punjab and Haryana, government procurement, transport networks and market access let farmers sell surplus rice; in Odisha, rice is grown mostly for family and local use, with traditional farming methods.
marking_scheme: One point on economic factors or farming practices: 1 mark

questions.question: Name one important beverage crop and specify the geographical conditions required for its growth.
answer_steps: Tea is an important beverage crop.
It needs a tropical or subtropical climate: warm, moist and frost-free throughout the year, with frequent showers evenly distributed.
It needs deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus and organic matter, and abundant cheap skilled labour.

questions.question: Name one staple crop of India and the regions where it is produced.
answer_steps: Rice is the staple food crop of a majority of Indians.
It is grown in the plains of north and north-east India, coastal areas and deltaic regions (West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala).
With canal and tubewell irrigation, it is also grown in less rainy Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.

questions.question: Enlist the various institutional reform programmes introduced by the government in the interest of farmers.
answer_steps: Land reforms: collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, co-operation and abolition of zamindari.
Crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease; Grameen banks, co-operative societies and banks for cheap loans; Kisan Credit Card and Personal Accident Insurance Scheme.
Weather bulletins and agricultural programmes on radio and TV, and minimum support prices to protect farmers from middlemen.

questions.question: Suggest the initiative taken by the government to ensure the increase in agricultural production.
answer_steps: Land reforms after Independence: consolidation of holdings, co-operation and abolition of zamindari.
The Green Revolution introduced HYV seeds, fertilisers and irrigation; the White Revolution (Operation Flood) raised milk production.
Crop insurance and cheap credit through Grameen banks, co-operatives, Kisan Credit Cards and PAIS.
Weather bulletins and farm programmes on radio and television spread knowledge.
Minimum support prices and procurement give farmers fair returns and protect them from speculators and middlemen.

questions.question: Describe the geographical conditions required for the growth of rice.
answer_steps: Rice is a kharif crop requiring high temperature, above 25°C.
It needs high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm.
In areas of less rainfall, it is grown with irrigation (Punjab, Haryana, western UP, parts of Rajasthan).
It grows in the plains of north and north-east India, coastal areas and deltaic regions, mostly on alluvial soil.
In Assam, West Bengal and Odisha, three crops (Aus, Aman, Boro) are grown in a year.

questions.question: Describe the three cropping seasons of India.
answer_steps: Rabi: sown October-December, harvested April-June; wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard; helped by winter rain from western temperate cyclones.
Kharif: sown with the monsoon, harvested September-October; paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean.
Zaid: a short summer season between rabi and kharif; watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops.

questions.question: Describe the conditions for growing cotton and name its major producing states.
answer_steps: Cotton grows well in the drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau.
It needs high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine; it is a kharif crop taking 6-8 months.
Major states: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

questions.question: Why are pulses important in Indian agriculture?
answer_steps: India is the largest producer and consumer of pulses; they are the main source of protein in a vegetarian diet.
They need less moisture and survive even in dry conditions.
Being leguminous (except arhar), they fix nitrogen from the air and restore soil fertility, so they are grown in rotation with other crops.

questions.question: Describe the four types of farming in India.
answer_steps: Primitive subsistence farming: slash-and-burn on small patches with hoe, dao and digging sticks and family labour; depends on monsoon and soil fertility; called jhumming in the north-east.
Intensive subsistence farming: in areas of high population, labour-intensive with high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation; inheritance divides land into small holdings.
Commercial farming: uses HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides; commercialisation varies, e.g. rice is commercial in Punjab and Haryana but subsistence in Odisha.
Plantation farming: a single crop on a large area, capital-intensive with migrant labour; produce used by industries.
Examples of plantation crops: tea in Assam and North Bengal, coffee in Karnataka, rubber, sugarcane and banana; it needs good transport linking plantations, industries and markets.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"Tea cultivation is an example of plantation agriculture. It is also an important beverage crop introduced in India initially by the British. Today, most of the tea plantations are owned by Indians. The tea plant grows well in tropical and subtropical climates endowed with deep and fertile well-drained soil, rich in humus and organic matter."* (NCERT)

(i) Who first introduced tea in India? (1)

(ii) What kind of soil suits tea? (1)

(iii) Why is tea processed within the garden, and what labour does it need? (2)
answer_steps: (i) The British.
(ii) Deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus and organic matter.
(iii) Tea leaves are processed within the garden to restore their freshness; tea is labour-intensive and needs abundant, cheap and skilled labour.
